title: What I Remember Now
subtitle: Lanternweald — sixth expansion pass
content:
The photograph was still facedown in the drawer.

I'd left it there when I first returned to the room beyond my old door. Back then, even the thought of seeing an unfamiliar face with a familiar smile had frightened me. I had closed the door, carried the green notebook to Tideglass, and told Maui I would come back when I chose.

Today I chose.

Maui walked with me to the arch but waited outside. He didn't ask who might be in the photograph. He didn't ask whether finding an old memory would change how I felt about him.

He carried his hook as though it had suddenly become the least useful tool in any world.

"I could stay nearby," he offered. "Extremely nearby. Or moderately nearby. I can become a small bird and—"

"No bird spying."

He made a face. "There goes the best part of the plan."

Mini Maui marched across his chest and held an imaginary sign reading *WAIT*. Maui looked down and sighed as though his own tattoos had betrayed him again.

"I am excellent at dramatic entrances," he said. "Not as gifted at dramatic staying outside."

"You can still be here when I come back."

"That's the idea."

His voice had grown quieter. There was something raw beneath the grin. He'd once been left alone long enough to mistake being needed for being loved. I knew that history didn't stop mattering because he'd learned to be considerate.

He took one step back from the arch, then raised his arms in an exaggerated flourish. "Go forth, mysterious person with excellent taste in demigods. I'll be right here, doing absolutely nothing interesting."

I laughed. It was exactly the sort of promise he found hardest to keep, and I trusted him to try.

I think he wanted to.

I loved him for asking instead, "Do you want me close enough to hear if you call?"

"Yes. But not inside yet."

He nodded.

I turned the key.

The room smelled of dust and laundry soap. The desk was exactly as I'd left it, except that the light had changed with the season. A small crack ran across the glaze of the cup beside the lamp. My old pen lay where I'd dropped it months earlier.

I opened the drawer.

The photograph showed a table. People sat around it, their faces blurred at the edges by years of handling. I recognized the shape of my own hand in the foreground, holding a mug. Someone had written on the back: *Ask for what you want.*

I stared at the words.

Then the memory came, not as a grand revelation but as a small, humiliating scene.

I was sitting at the table, telling people I didn't mind where we went. I did mind. I'd wanted to stay home, wanted quiet, wanted someone to notice I was overwhelmed. Instead I'd smiled and said anything was fine.

Later I'd been angry that nobody had read my mind.

I sat on the bed with the photograph in my lap.

That was it.

Not the lost name of a villain. Not proof I had been chosen to save the vale. Just evidence of a person who had been afraid to ask for ordinary care.

I laughed, then cried.

When the tears settled, I opened the green notebook and wrote down what I remembered.

*I used to confuse not asking with being easy to love.*

The words hurt.

I wrote another line.

*I don't want to do that anymore.*

A soft knock came from the hall.

"Jasper?"

"I'm here."

"Do you want company?"

I looked at the photograph.

"Yes."

Maui came in slowly. His eyes moved around the room, curious but careful.

I handed him the photograph.

"Do you recognize anyone?" he asked.

"Not all of them. I remember what was happening, though."

I told him about the table, the false agreement, and the anger I'd carried afterward. He listened with his hands resting open on his knees.

"That sounds lonely," he said.

"It was. I made it lonelier by pretending I wasn't asking for anything."

He looked at me.

"You're better at asking now."

"Sometimes."

"Sometimes is a start."

I smiled.

We went back to Tideglass that afternoon. I didn't take anything else from the room. I left the photograph in its drawer, facedown again, not because I was afraid of it but because I could return when I wanted.

At home, I made a list of wishes.

Not demands. Not promises other people were required to fulfill.

For Maui, I wished for laughter without an audience, dates we actually kept, and the ability to fight fairly when we made mistakes. For Iroh, tea without having to be wise. For Severus, a quiet room where his past wasn't on trial every night. For Aang, Katara, and Toph, separate time with each of them and a shared home that never felt like a vote on somebody's autonomy. For Danse, a workshop where care did not require a rank. For Greg, songs he could finish or leave unfinished without apology.

I wrote one more wish for myself.

*A day when I say what I need before I become angry that nobody knows.*

I read the list again before asking Maui to look at it. Some of the wishes were embarrassingly small: fresh bread when I was hungry, a day without the feeling of being watched, enough quiet to recognize a memory without somebody turning it into a clue.

At the bottom, I wrote a reminder about the photograph. The person beside me in it might have mattered deeply once. I could miss somebody without recognizing their face, and I could respect their privacy without rebuilding a story from fragments. I didn't have to show the picture to the whole archive just because it had survived.

I went back to the old room that afternoon, alone. The desk drawer still stuck when I pulled it. The photograph had curled slightly at one corner. I placed it in a clean paper sleeve and recorded where I'd found it, the way Neri had taught me to preserve a fragile object without pretending I'd authenticated its meaning.

There were other things in the drawer: a receipt for an ordinary loaf of bread, a loose button and a pencil with the end chewed flat. They moved me more than the photograph. Someone who'd been me had spent a morning shopping and repairing clothes. They hadn't known their life would someday become a question.

I sat on the floor until the room felt like a room again, not a trap.

When I returned to Tideglass, Maui was folding the clean sheets. He'd made a crooked stack and was glaring at the last pillowcase as though it had insulted him.

"Did you find what you wanted?" he asked.

"Not all of it. I found enough to know I want to come back later."

He nodded. "Would you like to be left alone?"

"Not right now. Could you sit with me while I decide which parts I want to tell you?"

He put the pillowcase down.

"I can do that."

And he did, without making the silence a heroic act.

I told him about the ordinary receipt, not the face in the photograph. I could hear the relief in my own voice when I realized he wasn't going to ask for the rest. I was still the same person who had told him I was ethically non-monogamous and preferred polyamory. His love didn't require an inventory of all the people I had loved, or all the people I might love later.

The afternoon faded while we sat at the kitchen table. He made us tea badly. I drank it anyway.

"Your tea tastes like the kettle lost an argument," I told him.

"Then you are welcome to make the next cup."

"I am. But I appreciate the effort."

He smiled, shy enough that I wanted to kiss him. I didn't yet. I had one more thing to say, and he waited.

Maui read the list only after I invited him.

He traced the edge of the page with one finger.

"That's a lot of people."

"Yes."

He smiled.

"And a lot of wishes."

"Also yes."

"Do you expect me to make all of them happen?"

"No. I don't even expect the people named to make their own wishes happen for me. I want to tell the truth about what I hope for, then listen to what they want."

He nodded.

"Then I have a wish."

"Tell me."

"Tomorrow morning, I want to sleep late with you. No meeting, no rescue, no heroic breakfast. Just us."

I grinned.

"I can do that."

He leaned closer.

"Can I kiss you?"

"Yes."

His kiss was soft at first, then warmer when I took his hand. We stayed at the kitchen table until the candles burned low, talking about ordinary things: the sea-glass garden, Lio's skiff, whether the next loaf should have less cinnamon.

When we finally went upstairs, we closed the door and kept the night private.

In the morning, Maui woke early.

He stayed in bed anyway.

I watched the first light move across the window and felt an unfamiliar peace.

The memory hadn't given me a complete past.

It had given me a better question to ask the future.

And this time I knew I was allowed to answer it.
